sources.title: National Archives, Declaration of Independence: A Transcription
sources.note: July 4, 1776 Declaration; National Archives transcription notes it reflects the Stone engraving and original spelling; the 1776 language of equality existed alongside exclusions.

sources.title: National Archives, The Constitution: How Did it Happen?
sources.note: 1787 Philadelphia convention, September signature, slavery compromise, ratification and government framework; constitution did not grant equal rights to all residents.

sources.title: National Archives, Congress and the Bill of Rights in History and Today
sources.note: First ten constitutional amendments ratified in 1791; result of Federalist and Anti-Federalist debate over rights and central power.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, American Indian Removal
sources.note: Treaties, fraud, intimidation and violence removed roughly 100,000 American Indians from 1830 to 1850; created with tribal consultation, including Cherokee Nation.

sources.title: National Park Service, Trail of Tears History and Culture
sources.note: 1830 Removal Act, Cherokee majority opposed New Echota treaty and forced 1838 removal; specific nations and survival, not disappearance.

sources.title: National Museum of African American History and Culture, Defining Freedom
sources.note: Slavery, 1865 Thirteenth Amendment, Reconstruction, Black Codes, 1866 civil rights law, Jim Crow and long Black political struggle.

sources.title: National Park Service, Groveton School House
sources.note: Local Virginia one-room school with about 30 pupils; farm-season absences, recess games, and racial inequality in travel distance and schooling; local example only.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Rosenwald Schools
sources.note: Black communities and allies built improved schools in segregated South during early twentieth century; local initiative amid unequal public funding.

sources.title: Smithsonian Food History, Cooking Up History: Chicken Croquettes
sources.note: Smithsonian food-history handout: American women documented changing recipes in late eighteenth and nineteenth-century cookbooks; recipes represent literate cooks and particular households.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, History of Sweatshops 1880-1940
sources.note: Immigrant garment work in tenements, hazardous conditions, family labor and varied outcomes; specific industrial sector and period.

sources.title: National Park Service, Immigrant Inspector at Ellis Island
sources.note: Ellis Island inspection involved face-to-face questions, passenger manifests and exclusion criteria; not all immigrants entered through Ellis Island.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Seward Privy Project
sources.note: Excavated three early Seward, Alaska outhouses circa 1905-1920; archaeological privies can preserve discarded everyday objects, a local case.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, Bathing and Body Soaps
sources.note: Bathing habits, nineteenth-century promotion of bathing and unequal access to running water in working-class tenements.

sources.title: CDC, Ten Great Public Health Achievements: United States 1900-1999
sources.note: Twentieth-century water sanitation, vaccination and other public-health gains, with reductions in waterborne disease; population-level history, not universal access.

sources.title: National Archives, Nineteenth Amendment
sources.note: Ratified August 18, 1920 and barred denial of vote on account of sex; hard-won suffrage, with other barriers continuing.

sources.title: National Archives, Guide to House Records: Treaty of Paris 1898
sources.note: Treaty following Spanish-American War: Spain ceded Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam to United States and relinquished Cuba; imperial expansion with distinct later statuses.

sources.title: National Archives, Joint Address to Congress Leading to War with Japan
sources.note: December 7, 1941 Pearl Harbor attack and December 8 US declaration of war, entry into World War II.

sources.title: National Archives, Executive Order 9066
sources.note: 1942 order led to forced removal and incarceration of about 122,000 Japanese Americans, including citizens; 1988 official apology and partial restitution.

sources.title: National Park Service, The Story of Brown
sources.note: School desegregation struggle and civil rights movement; Brown v. Board and later protests, with 1964 Civil Rights Act milestone.

sources.title: National Archives, Voting Rights Act 1965
sources.note: August 6, 1965 act targeted literacy tests and other discriminatory voting barriers; based on civil rights organizing and Selma violence.

sources.title: NASA, Apollo 11
sources.note: 1969 Apollo 11 crewed lunar landing and return; Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins; national effort involved many workers beyond astronauts.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, School Days Lunch Box
sources.note: Specific 1983 Aladdin steel lunch box decorated with Disney school scenes; object reflects commercial childhood culture, not all lunches or families.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The 1776 Declaration marks political independence as a claim; British recognition came later and the federal Constitution was signed in 1787, ratified and implemented afterward. The imported polygon begins 1783 and is not a certification of 1776 control. The United States remains a continuing state, so no invented dissolution or successor is supplied.

Indigenous nations predate and continue across United States expansion. Indian removal and 1898 overseas expansion are named as exercises of state power affecting existing populations. U.S. map color must not imply one culture, full consent or homogeneous sovereignty.

The English writing sample is an exact short phrase from NARA's Stone engraving transcription of the Declaration, with its transcription basis stated. It is one public written language, not a list of every language used in the country.

Groveton school and Rosenwald schools are place/period-specific; cookbooks represent particular literate kitchens; Seward privies are archaeological evidence from one Alaskan town; the 1983 lunch box is a single manufactured object. None are national household surveys.

National Archives and NMAAHC distinguish 1865 legal abolition from the continued Black struggle against Black Codes and Jim Crow. The 1920 amendment barred sex-based voting exclusions but racial suppression continued, leading to the 1965 act. The 1942 Japanese American incarceration is named, not euphemized.

All narrative author-checked and awaiting independent review. Imported polygons unchanged and unverified. This North America ID was unassigned in the coverage queue; QWEN-owned Asia-only IDs remain untouched.

proposedOverrides.summary: The United States declared independence in 1776 and built a federal republic. Its history includes Indigenous sovereignty and forced removal, slavery and emancipation, migration, industry, struggles for equal rights, science and changing daily life. Families and communities have never shared one experience. The state continues today, so the map shows changing periods rather than a single ending.
